subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 10 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. Instead of writing a story on paper, they bring a story to life on a screen: you choose characters and a background, make the characters talk in speech bubbles, and make them take turns so they have a proper conversation.

The source textbook names ScratchJr directly, so we use exactly the tool it intends. The star of the show is the Say block, which makes a character speak. That is how a back-and-forth conversation is built. The free tool for this unit is ScratchJr, a colourful app made especially for you aged five to seven. There is no code to read and nothing to type in as commands — you simply drag picture blocks together and tap the green flag to watch your story play. To make two characters talk to each other, you use messages: one character finishes speaking and sends a coloured message, and the other character is waiting for that colour and starts speaking when it arrives.

First, you learn to predict what an algorithm will do. An algorithm takes something in (the input) and gives something back out (the output), and we can work out the output ourselves by doing the steps the way the computer would. Second, you learn to test as you build — to check each character's part works before moving on, so mistakes do not pile up. Third, you learn to debug: to find the one block that is wrong and fix it.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Explain that an algorithm has an input (what goes in) and an output (what comes out).
Predict what an algorithm will do by working through the steps like a computer (for example, a small number machine).
Make a character speak in ScratchJr using the Say block.
Make two characters take turns to talk, using Send Message and Start on Message with matching colours.
Add a second scene using a Go to Page block.
Test a program while writing it — check each character's part works before moving on.
Say what a bug is, and debug a short story by finding and fixing one mistake.
Plan a short story as an algorithm and turn it into a running program.

toolkit.name: ScratchJr
steps: Open ScratchJr on a tablet.
Tap the house, then tap the plus to start a new project.
Drag the coloured picture blocks together to make your character move.
Tap the green flag to run it.

concepts.title: Input and output: the number machine (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm takes something in and gives something back out. What we put in is the input; what comes out is the output. If we follow the steps ourselves, just like the computer, we can predict the output before we even run it.

We put a number IN one side, the machine does its job, and a number comes OUT the other side.
concepts.example: Find one real example of input and output: the number machine around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you predict the output of a one-step machine? Can you put story steps into a sensible order?

concepts.title: Make a character talk: the Say block
concepts.explanation:
Today we open ScratchJr and meet the Say block. The Say block makes a character speak — the words pop up in a speech bubble. This is how we tell a story on the screen. The yellow Start on Green Flag block starts everything when we tap the green flag.

tap the blue plus to add a character — this is Nadia. The yellow block starts things.
concepts.example: The purple Say block makes Nadia talk. Open a new project and tap the picture button at the top to choose a Background (somewhere at school).
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drag the Say block, type a short line, and run it with the green flag? Can you point to the green-flag block and say it starts the program? Can you add a background and a character?

concepts.title: Taking turns: messages, and testing as we build
concepts.explanation:
To make two characters talk to each other, they must take turns. In ScratchJr we do this with messages. One character finishes talking and sends a coloured message with Send Message. The other character is waiting for that colour with Start on Message, and it starts talking when the message arrives. The colours must match. We also learn to test as we build: check Nadia's part works, then add Leo, then check again.

Act it out first, with no screen. Leo is watching for orange; the moment he sees it, he says his line. Now build it in ScratchJr.
concepts.example: Add Nadia and give her Try it with a mismatch for fun — Nadia holds up orange but Leo is only watching for red — and Leo stays silent. You instantly see: the colours must match.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you check the colours match? Can you test one part before adding the next? Can you build a Send Message on one character and a matching Start on Message on the other?

concepts.title: Two scenes, and debugging together
concepts.explanation:
A story can have more than one scene. In ScratchJr, each page is a scene. A Go to Page block turns the page to a new background. We also learn to debug: a bug is a mistake in a program, and debugging is finding the wrong block and fixing it — and it is easier with a friend.

Set Page 2 to a new background — the date table. Add a Go to Page block at the end of Leo's reply so the story moves on after the greeting Show that a project can have two pages (tap the page thumbnails on the right).
concepts.example: Find one real example of two scenes, and debugging together around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you find the mismatched message colour and say what it should be? Can you see a bug as a fixable mistake, not a disaster? Can you add a second page and a Go to Page block?

concepts.title: Be a storyteller: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
They plan a short story, build it in ScratchJr with two characters that take turns, test as they go, add a second scene, and debug a tricky part with a partner. This session and the Mini-Project go hand in hand.

Now you are the storyteller. You will tell the story of two friends at Ehel Academy.
concepts.example: First plan what you say, then build it, testing as you go — and if there is a bug, find it with your partner. Keep the story short — a greeting and one reply is a complete story.
concepts.checkYourself: Did you test as you built and fix the bug in Part C? Did you work well with your partner? Does you plan before building? Do the two characters take turns with matching messages?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

The answer 6 the machine gives us.

vocabulary.example: The steps a character does in order.

vocabulary.example: The ScratchJr blocks that play the story.

vocabulary.meaning: The block that makes a character speak.
A signal one character sends so another can start.
vocabulary.example: Leo waits for the orange message, then talks.

vocabulary.example: Page 1 is the door; Page 2 is the date table.

vocabulary.meaning: To find and fix the mistake.
vocabulary.example: We matched the colours, and it worked.

commonMistakes: Both characters will just talk on their own.
They will not take turns by themselves. One must Send Message and the other must Start on Message with the same colour — that is what makes them wait and reply.
The message colour does not matter.
It matters completely. Send orange but wait for red, and nobody answers. The colours must match.
The Say block will read the words out loud.
No — Say shows the words in a speech bubble on the screen. It does not make a voice. (There is a separate record-sound block for voices, which we do not need here.)
A bug means I am bad at this.
Not at all. Everyone makes bugs, even expert programmers. A bug is just a mistake we can find and fix.
I should build the whole story, then test at the end.
It is much easier to test each part as you build. Then if something breaks, you know it was the part you just added.
The green-flag block can go anywhere.
The Start on Green Flag block must sit at the top of a character's blocks, or they will not run when you tap the flag.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Which block makes a character talk? ([ ] Go to Page)
Nadia sends an orange message. What colour must Leo's Start on Message block be so he can hear it?
Put this talk in order. Write 1, 2, 3 in the boxes.
Explain the key idea in two scenes, and debugging together, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A story can have more than one scene. In ScratchJr, each page is a scene. A Go to Page block turns the page to a new background. We also learn to debug: a bug is a mistake in a program, and debugging is finding the wrong block and fixing it — and it is easier with a friend.

Set Page 2 to a new background — the date table. Add a Go to Page block at the end of Leo's reply so the story moves on after the greeting Show that a project can have two pages (tap the page thumbnails on the right).

project.title: Unit 10 Project: Be a Storyteller
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Storyteller into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a storyteller project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I planned my story in order on the storyboard.
I made Nadia talk with a Say block.
I made Leo reply using a matching-colour message.
I tested each part as I built it.
I added a second scene with Go to Page.
I found and fixed the bug with my partner.
I added one more block to make it better.

selfAssessment: I can explain that an algorithm has an input (what goes in) and an output (what comes out).
I can predict what an algorithm will do by working through the steps like a computer (for example, a small number machine).
I can make a character speak in ScratchJr using the Say block.
I can make two characters take turns to talk, using Send Message and Start on Message with matching colours.
I can add a second scene using a Go to Page block.
I can test a program while writing it — check each character's part works before moving on.
I can say what a bug is, and debug a short story by finding and fixing one mistake.
I can plan a short story as an algorithm and turn it into a running program.
